exhibits.title: The Cauldron That Stirs Only the Past
exhibits.text:
At the climax of the Gallery stands a great silver cauldron, and into it a keeper may feed a long reel of moving portrait — eighty-one frames of silvered glass, a full five seconds of enchanted motion. The cauldron does not keep them all. It reduces the reel to a short, concentrated essence — a handful of latent frames that hold the whole of what happened — and from that essence the reel can be brewed back at will. This is the CAUSAL 3D VAE, the workhorse that lets the Gallery's longest portraits exist at all.

Recall the still-portrait cauldron two floors below, in the Latent Vault. The image VAE took a picture of 512x512x3 and pressed its two SPATIAL dimensions some eight times smaller a side, down to a latent of 64x64x4, whence a decoder could restore the full picture. It compressed WHERE things sat in the frame by exploiting the redundancy between neighbouring PIXELS — a patch of sky is much like the sky beside it, so the frame need not be stored pixel by pixel. For a single still, TIME did not exist; there was nothing to compress along it.

A moving portrait has a time axis, and here the naive keeper WASTES. Run the old still-cauldron on each frame alone and you compress space handsomely but not one whisper of time. Yet consecutive frames of a moving portrait are nearly the same picture — frame five is very nearly frame six — so keeping eighty-one separate latents squanders capacity on what barely changed, and leaves eighty-one latent frames for temporal attention to labour over at its ruinous T-squared cost. The remedy rhymes exactly with the spatial one: as space is compressed by exploiting neighbouring PIXELS, so time should be compressed by exploiting neighbouring FRAMES.

The cauldron does it with THREE-DIMENSIONAL convolutions. Where the still-cauldron slid its little reading-kernel across only (H, W), this one slides across (T, H, W) — across time as well as space. Because each 3D kernel spans a FEW FRAMES at once, it merges their information, and so the encoder can downsample the time axis just as it downsamples height and width. Wan's cauldron compresses time about four-fold and space about eight-fold a side: eighty-one input frames become roughly twenty-one latent frames. Now temporal attention runs over twenty-one tokens, not eighty-one — the T-squared burden lightened by an order and more.

But mark WHICH frames the kernel drinks from, for therein lies the whole enchantment. Study the plinths and the ledger around this cauldron: an ordinary 3D convolution reaches to BOTH sides of the present, into the future as well as the past — and that single greed would make the longest portraits impossible. This cauldron is CAUSAL: it stirs only what has already happened. That is the one change, borrowed straight from the decoder's causal mask in the Compass and Clock, and from it flows everything that lets a moving portrait run long.

exhibits.title: Compressing Space AND Time
exhibits.text:
The still-portrait VAE compressed only SPACE: 512x512x3 pressed to 64x64x4, the two spatial dimensions squeezed about eight times smaller a side by exploiting the redundancy between neighbouring PIXELS. A moving portrait adds a time axis (T, H, W, C), and here a per-frame stilling wastes: neighbouring FRAMES are nearly identical (frame five is nearly frame six), so eighty-one separate latents hoard capacity on redundancy, and eighty-one latent frames leave temporal attention its full T-squared bill.

The 3D VAE compresses TIME as well. Its convolutions slide over (T, H, W) rather than only (H, W); because each kernel spans several frames, it merges their information, letting the encoder downsample time exactly as it downsamples height and width. The two compressions are one idea wearing two coats: space exploits neighbouring pixels, time exploits neighbouring frames, both through 3D convolutions over (T, H, W).

Wan's numbers: about 4x compression in time, about 8x a side in space. Eighty-one input frames collapse to roughly twenty-one latent frames. Temporal attention then runs over twenty-one tokens instead of eighty-one — a decisive cut to the T-squared cost that made long reels so dear.

exhibits.title: The Bilateral Problem
exhibits.text:
An ordinary 3D convolution is even-handed: to read frame t it reaches equally into the past AND the future, its kernel spanning [t-2, t-1, t, t+1, t+2]. That symmetry is fatal to a moving portrait that must run long.

First, it forbids streaming. To encode or decode frame t you must already possess frames t+1 and t+2 — the future. So the whole video must be held at once, start to finish, in memory; you cannot generate or decode it incrementally, chunk after chunk, because every chunk would demand frames that do not yet exist.

Second, it breaks variable length. The boundary arithmetic of a bilateral kernel assumes a fixed window open on both sides; feed a reel of unexpected length and the two-sided book-keeping at the ends no longer closes cleanly.

So the very reach that lets a normal 3D conv see context in both directions is the shackle: it pins the model to whole, fixed-length videos held entire in VRAM. The Gallery needs a kernel that never looks forward.

exhibits.title: What 'Causal' Means
exhibits.text:
A CAUSAL 3D convolution looks only at the current frame and the past — never the future. Where the ordinary kernel spanned [t-2, t-1, t, t+1, t+2], the causal kernel spans [t-2, t-1, t]: present and past alone. Nothing downstream in time is permitted to inform frame t.

This is not a new invention but an old law re-applied. It is precisely the DECODER'S CAUSAL MASK from the Compass and Clock — the rule that a token may attend only to tokens at or before its own position — carried over from attention onto temporal convolution. There, position t could not peek at position t+1; here, frame t cannot peek at frame t+1.

What of the very first frame, which has no past to lean on? The kernel PADS: the sequence is extended backward with copies (or zeros) so the arithmetic still closes, and the opening frame effectively conditions on itself. Every subsequent frame conditions on the true frames that preceded it. The window slides forward through time and never once turns its head.

exhibits.title: Why Causality Unlocks Everything
exhibits.text:
Forbid the future and four gifts fall out at once.

SLIDING-WINDOW DECODING. Since decoding frame t needs only its past, you may decode through a small sliding window and never hold the whole reel in memory. This is what keeps VRAM bounded on long portraits — a sixty-second latent will not fit decoded all at once, but a window of it always will.

STREAMING, AUTOREGRESSIVE GENERATION. Because no frame depends on what comes after, you may generate and decode as you go: brew chunk one, then brew chunk two conditioned on chunk one's tail, onward without end. This causal structure is precisely what makes the overlap-chunking of the Stitcher's Table possible.

VARIABLE LENGTH. A causal kernel needs no fixed bilateral window; each frame simply conditions on however much past exists. So the cauldron accepts any number of frames, and Wan may take a duration as a dial.

CLEAN CHUNK HANDOVERS. Because compression respects the arrow of time, the tail of one chunk is valid 'past' for the next, so segments join without a seam in the latent.

One honest caveat, spoken plainly: the causal VAE makes long reels POSSIBLE, but it cannot make them PERFECT. Chunked generation still accumulates drift across segments — each chunk remembers only a short tail, not the whole portrait — and that slow wandering is a debt the VAE alone can never repay.

exhibits.title: The Cauldron's Ledger
exhibits.text:
Being a full accounting of how the Gallery came to compress time itself, set down for the keeper who would understand the cauldron end to end.

I. RECALL THE STILL CAULDRON. Two floors below, in the Latent Vault, the image VAE performed a single trick: it took a picture of shape 512x512x3 and pressed its two SPATIAL dimensions about eight times smaller a side, yielding a latent of 64x64x4, from which a decoder could restore the full image. It compressed WHERE — the layout of the frame — by exploiting the redundancy of neighbouring PIXELS. This is why the whole of Stable Diffusion could be run in a small latent rather than in ruinous pixel space. For a single still there was no time axis; there was nothing to compress along it.

II. THE PER-FRAME WASTE. A moving portrait is a stack of frames, shape (T, H, W, C). The lazy keeper runs the still cauldron on each frame independently — and compresses not one instant of time. Two costs follow. First, capacity is squandered: consecutive frames are nearly identical (frame five is very nearly frame six), so eighty-one separate latents store the same near-picture over and over. Second, the temporal sequence stays long: eighty-one latent frames is eighty-one tokens for temporal attention, and attention pays the square of its length. The cure must rhyme with the spatial one — as space is compressed by leaning on neighbouring pixels, time should be compressed by leaning on neighbouring frames.

III. THE 3D CONVOLUTION COMPRESSES TIME. The remedy is to slide the reading-kernel not over (H, W) but over (T, H, W) — over time as well as space. A 3D convolution spans a FEW FRAMES at once and merges their information, and so the encoder may downsample the time axis just as it downsamples height and width. Wan's VAE presses time about four-fold and space about eight-fold a side: eighty-one input frames become roughly twenty-one latent frames. Temporal attention now labours over twenty-one tokens rather than eighty-one — the T-squared cost cut hard. Space compression exploits neighbouring pixels; time compression exploits neighbouring frames; both are the same 3D convolution over (T, H, W).

IV. THE BILATERAL PROBLEM. But an ordinary 3D convolution is even-handed. To read frame t it reaches to BOTH sides — [t-2, t-1, t, t+1, t+2] — into the future as much as the past. That greed carries two curses. It forbids streaming: to encode or decode frame t you must already hold frames t+1 and t+2, so the WHOLE video must sit in memory at once and cannot be produced incrementally. And it breaks variable length: the boundary arithmetic of a two-sided kernel presumes a fixed window open on both ends, which frays when the reel is longer or shorter than expected.

V. THE CAUSAL FIX. Make the kernel CAUSAL: let it span only [t-2, t-1, t], present and past, never the future. This is nothing more than the decoder's causal mask from the Compass and Clock — a position may attend only to itself and what precedes it — carried from attention onto temporal convolution. At the very start, where there is no past, the kernel PADS, and the first frame conditions on itself; every later frame conditions on the true frames before it. The window slides forward and never turns its head.

VI. THE FOUR UNLOCKS. From that one refusal of the future, four gifts fall. (1) SLIDING-WINDOW DECODING: decoding frame t needs only its past, so a small window suffices and VRAM stays bounded even on a sixty-second reel that could never be decoded whole. (2) STREAMING, AUTOREGRESSIVE GENERATION: no frame depends on the future, so you brew chunk after chunk, each conditioned on the last one's tail — the very mechanism the Stitcher's Table uses to extend a reel past its trained horizon. (3) VARIABLE LENGTH: with no fixed bilateral window, each frame conditions on whatever past exists, so any frame count is welcome and duration becomes a dial. (4) CLEAN HANDOVERS: because compression honours the arrow of time, the tail of one chunk is valid past for the next, and segments join without a latent seam.

VII. THE RESIDUAL DEBT. Speak the caveat honestly. The causal VAE makes the long reel POSSIBLE; it does not make it PERFECT. Chunked generation still accumulates DRIFT across segments — each chunk carries only a short tail of memory, never the whole portrait — so colour, motion, and lighting wander slowly the longer you run. That accumulating error is precisely the debt the cauldron cannot settle: it compresses time faithfully, but it holds no global memory of the whole video. What the causal VAE grants is bounded memory, variable length, and clean streaming; what it leaves for other arts to solve is the long, patient drift.

exhibits.caption: The reel of 81 frames enters a 3D causal-convolution encoder that slides over (T, H, W); because every kernel spans only the present and past — never the future — it compresses time about 4x and space about 8x a side into roughly 21 latent frames. That causal structure lets the decoder work through a sliding window over past frames alone, so memory stays bounded and generation may stream chunk by chunk. As a bonus, temporal attention now runs over 21 tokens rather than 81.

exhibits.title: The Causal Window, Read Three Ways
exhibits.caption: Three readings of the cauldron's craft, keeper. (a) An ordinary 3D convolution is even-handed: to read frame t it drinks from both sides, [t-2 ... t+2], reaching into the future — so the whole reel must be held at once. The CAUSAL kernel spans only [t-2 ... t], present and past; it never turns its head forward. That single restraint is the decoder's causal mask from the Compass and Clock, carried onto temporal convolution. (b) The encoder slides over (T, H, W) rather than only (H, W), and so compresses time as well as space: eighty-one frames of 512x512x3 become roughly twenty-one latent frames of 64x64xc — about eight-fold a side in space, four-fold in time. Temporal attention then labours over twenty-one tokens, not eighty-one — near fifteen-fold fewer pairs, for its cost grows as the square of the length. (c) Because decoding frame t needs only its past, the decoder works through a sliding window and streams chunk by chunk; peak memory stays FLAT however long the reel, where a bilateral kernel's would swell without bound. The numbers are Wan's, and representative.
